The split inside type A is carried in the card briefs, not in a type: problem led (symptom, cause in the wind, the ground or the timber, consequence) for fence repairs with storm damage as the anchor, concrete posts and gravel boards, dog proof, security and acoustic fencing; desire led (the customer's situation, never an invented symptom; the library's desire_led column, which swaps in service_page_blocks.A.desire) for timber, composite, closeboard, panel, picket and hit and miss fencing, metal fencing and railings, made to measure fencing, garden gates, automatic gates and bin and log stores; specification led (what the animal or the site does to a fence, written into the 'on a specification led page' line of each service card) for agricultural and stock, equestrian, post and rail, electric, chain link and temporary fencing; schedule led (what slips and when, the reason in the timber or the weather) for fence staining and treatment. faq_slots.answer_brief: From [QUOTE_FREE] and [CV: quote_method].

faq_slots.question: How do your quotes work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.question: How long does it take to put up a new fence?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The trade facts give no standard duration for any fencing job, so give what decides it and no number unless confirmed: the length of the run, what has to come out first (an old fence, its posts and their concrete), the ground the holes go into, how the posts and panels get to the garden, and the weather for setting posts. Weather can move the days.

faq_slots.question: Why has my fence started to lean?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words: a post gone soft where it comes out of the soil, concrete that has worked loose in ground that shrinks in a dry summer and swells when wet, a solid run taking the whole wind on an open side. Then what the local ground or exposure adds, then the fix, which starts at the post and not the panel.

faq_slots.question: Can a storm damaged fence be repaired, or does it all need replacing?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts fence repairs rows: a repair can keep a run whose other posts are still firm, and a new panel on a failed post leaves the fault where it was. What decides it is whether the posts either side of the damage are still firm at the ground: a few new posts with the sound panels rehung where they are, or the run replaced where the posts along it have all gone soft. Never which neighbour pays (the fact row: a blown down fence is not automatically next door's bill), never a named storm.

faq_slots.question: Whose fence is it, mine or my neighbour's?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts fact rows only: there is no rule that the fence on the left or the right is yours; the deeds decide; a T mark on a plan can show who looks after a boundary but does not settle it on its own; the title plan shows a general line, not where each post stands. The finished face turned outward is a custom, not a law. Where it is unclear, a word with next door before anything comes down. Never legal advice, never a guess at which side.

faq_slots.question: Do I need planning permission for a new fence?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": most back garden fences need none up to the usual height; the limit is lower where the boundary runs beside a road with traffic on it, and its pavement counts, so a front fence is usually the lower one; the height is taken from the ground and trellis on top counts towards it; a replacement can usually keep an existing greater height; a listed home, and an estate where the right has been taken away, need a check first; a conservation area does not change the heights but taking an old boundary down there can need permission. The two heights themselves only as the rows give them and only on a page whose prompt carries the rows; otherwise no height at all. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it. Never an Act's or an order's name.

cards.title: A fence down or leaning after the wind
cards.brief: Problem led, the storm anchor: a panel out, a post snapped at the ground, a run leaning after a gale (the trade facts signs row for fence repairs). Write the diagnosis, never the drama. The one cause this card makes: a post gone soft where it comes out of the ground, so the wind pushed it over; a panel lifted out of its slot on an otherwise firm run is a different, smaller job, and the card says so. What it says about the rest of the run: posts put in together, in the same ground, tend to go soft at the same time, so the posts on each side of the damage get looked at before one is replaced (the done badly row: a new panel on a failed post leaves the fault in place). What the fix usually involves, from the fence repairs stages: the failed part found, the section made safe, the posts replaced or refixed and the sound panels rehung, or the run replaced where every post has gone. What the business does on site only from confirmed practices (photos_of_faults, extra_work_agreed_first). Never a named storm, never which neighbour pays (the fact row: a blown down fence is not automatically next door's bill), never storm proof.
cards.mechanism: a post gone soft where it comes out of the ground

cards.title: Overlooked, open to the road, or both
cards.brief: A situation card, desire led, never a fault invented for it: next door's upstairs windows look onto where the household sits, the front garden has nothing between the lawn and the pavement, a low chain link run from when the estate was built, a side gate that never closed properly. The one cause this card makes: a boundary set for how the house was once used, not for how this household uses it. What decides the answer: what the fence has to do (cover where they sit, mark the front, keep a dog or a toddler in), how much wind the run takes (a solid fence takes the whole of it; boards fixed alternately on the two faces let the wind pass between them, from the hit and miss row; prefabricated panels do not suit the most exposed runs, from the fact row on exposed locations, no figure), and the height that usually applies (lower where the boundary runs beside a road with traffic on it, its pavement included; higher elsewhere), from the trade facts rule rows with usually, never the order's name and no figure the rows do not give. What the work gives them, in plain words: closeboard built board by board on site, panels between posts, hit and miss, picket, metal railings, a gate, whichever does that job, named only where the services list has the page. Never a lifestyle pitch, never security sold on fear.
cards.mechanism: a boundary set for how the house was once used

cards.title: When the fence has one job to do
cards.brief: Function and specification led in one card: the fence is bought for what it must hold in or keep out. The one cause this card makes: pressure the fence was never built to take, from the animal, the people or the noise on the other side of it. Say what each does to a fence and what answers it, from the trade facts rows for that service, and name only the services the client has: a dog that digs under or pushes through finds the gap under the gate, the hole beside a post, the loose bottom edge (the dog proof rows: close mesh or a solid face, the bottom edge secured, the gate detail made for that dog; no universal height or gap, because the facts verify none); a horse leans on a rail, rubs along it and chews it, so post and rail is fixed so that a pushing horse presses the rails against the posts, and anything projecting is a hazard (the equestrian rows); sheep and cattle put their weight on netting, so stock fencing stands or falls on its end posts and the tension in the wires (the agricultural rows); a yard or a building site that must stay shut gets a tested system with its own matching gates, because an untested part put into a certified run undoes it (the security rows), sold on what the fence does and never on fear, crime figures or invented break ins; road noise is cut by a barrier with no gaps, its joints sealed and the boards close fitting (the acoustic rows), with no figure for how much quieter the garden will be (the fact row: a laboratory figure is not a garden figure). The customer's words throughout: the dog, the horses, the sheep, the yard, the road; never perimeter or specification.
cards.mechanism: pressure the fence was never built to take

cards.title: Timber going grey, green or soft
cards.brief: Schedule led, the upkeep group (fence staining and treatment): what slips and when. What the customer sees, from the trade facts signs row: a coating peeling, bare patches, timber that looks wet long after the rain has gone, boards going green on the shaded face. Say first what is normal: new timber silvering in its first year is the sun, not a fault. The one cause this card makes: timber left bare to the weather once the coating has worn through, so the rain gets into the surface and the cut ends (the skipped row). When treatment is due, in the timber and the weather, never in the diary: when the timber is dry through and the maker's conditions for the product hold (the staining stages: the timber dried as the product requires, the coats applied in the maker's weather), never a fixed interval, because the facts verify none. A coat put on damp timber fails early (the done badly row). A brush on treatment never replaces the pressure treatment a post needs where it goes into the ground (the done badly and fact rows), so a soft post at the ground is card 1's job, not this card's. A product only from [CV: materials_methods]; a return visit for recoating only where the services list has it.
cards.mechanism: timber left bare to the weather

cards.title: What comes out first
cards.brief: An old fence, its posts and the concrete they were set in, rubble under the line, a hedge in the way: what has to come out and go away before a post goes in (the trade facts price rows: removal and disposal of old fencing, buried post removal, old foundations). Say why each adds time. No figure.

cards.title: Posts, panels and gates you choose
cards.brief: Concrete posts against timber, closeboard built on site against panels, a gate in the run, a higher treatment on the timber, railings made to the opening (the trade facts price rows: post type, treatment, gate openings, fabrication and finish). Why one costs more than another, in plain words; a named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

faq_slots.question: How do I get a quote for a new fence?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends (roughly how long the run is, photos, which boundary), what the business looks at (the line, the levels, what comes out, how the materials get in), what comes back. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: Can you put up a fence at any time of year?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing cells: fencing goes in all year where the ground allows it. What the weather changes, with the reason in the ground, the concrete or the timber: post concrete sets more slowly in the cold (the concrete posts row: the initial set depends on temperature); staining and treatment wait for timber that is dry through and the maker's conditions; a hedge along the line is checked for nests before it is cut back (a stage of the job in the rows, written as this business's own practice only when nesting_bird_check is confirmed); a countryside hedge has its own cutting season, said as usually and without the rule's name. Nothing about autumn being busy or booking ahead. No dates, no promise about the weather.

faq_symptom.frame: [SYMPTOM]: why does it happen, and what can be done?
faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom (a leaning run, posts rotting at the ground, panels blowing out, a gate that drags) and its linked local issue, answered as asked. Say first when it is normal (new timber silvering, a panel that rattles in a gale and is back in its slot by morning) and then what is not. Then the usual cause here in the wind, the ground or the timber, in plain words; what the local exposure or soil adds (an open edge of town, clay that shrinks in a dry summer, low ground where holes fill with water) only from the research; and what the business does about it, starting at the post. One figure at most.

problem_card.title: What the autumn gales leave behind
problem_card.brief: After the autumn and winter gales. Say first what is normal: a panel lifted out of its slot and dropped back in, boards rattling in the wind, timber dark with the wet; then what is not: a post snapped at the ground, a run that leans a little more each windy day, a gate that no longer meets its post (the trade facts signs rows for fence repairs and panel fencing). The one cause this card makes: the wind finding the weakest point in the run, a post already soft at the ground or a solid panel on a run too exposed for it (the fact row on exposed locations, no figure). The reason in the timber and the weather, never in the season being busy: wet ground through the winter softens what was already going. What getting it looked at involves, from the fence repairs stages (the failed part found, the section made safe, posts replaced or refixed, sound panels rehung); what the business does only from confirmed practices. Never a named storm, never which neighbour pays, never storm proof.
problem_card.mechanism: the wind finding the weakest point in the run

faq_slot.question: Is winter a bad time to have a fence put up?
faq_slot.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing cells: fencing goes in through the winter where the ground allows it. What waits and why, in the ground, the concrete or the timber: post concrete sets more slowly in the cold; staining and treatment wait for timber that is dry through and the maker's conditions; a composite system goes up only within its maker's conditions. Nothing about the diary. No dates, no promise about the weather.

items.title: Finding pipes and cables before we dig

items.brief: The removal stage from the trade facts, where the row has it: the old panels, posts and their concrete out of the ground. Name only what the row gives; what happens to the waste only from confirmed practices (waste_removal).

items.title: Digging and setting the posts
items.brief: The post stage from the trade facts: holes dug, posts set, timber or concrete as the materials cell names them for this service. No depth or figure (the rows give none), and never a standard's number.

items.title: The rails, boards or panels
items.brief: The central stage from the trade facts: rails fixed, boards or panels fitted, mesh hung and tensioned, the gate hung, named as the trade names it for this service.

items.title: Gravel boards, caps and finishing

cards.title: The first thing you notice
cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the trade facts signs row for this service, in their words: a panel rattling, a board lifting, a rail hanging, a gate that drags, a post that moves when pushed. The one cause this card makes: a part that has worked loose or given way, a fixing, a rail or a post, so the rest of the bay is carrying it. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: specific, never alarming. On a specification led page (agricultural and stock, equestrian, post and rail, electric, chain link and temporary fencing) the card is what the animal or the site does to the fence: netting sagging where sheep push at it, a rail broken by a leaning horse, mesh gone slack as the tension is lost, no pulse on the tester with grass against the strand, a temporary panel pushed off its foot, from that service's signs row. On a schedule led page (fence staining and treatment) the card is what slips and when: a coating peeling, bare patches, timber that looks wet after the rain has gone, with the reason in the timber and the weather from the timing cell, never in the customer's diary.
cards.mechanism: a part that has worked loose or given way

cards.title: A lean that is getting worse
cards.brief: A post or a whole run that leans a little more with every windy week. The one cause this card makes: a post moving in its hole, because the ground round it has shrunk, washed out or been worked loose, so the panels on each side twist and the lean grows. Not a post rotted through at the ground: the category page owns that cause. Say what the job does underneath so the post stays put, from the trade facts stages and the done badly row for this service (the hole dug and the post set in concrete as the materials cell names it; concrete posts where the client offers them; a gravel board keeping the panel off the soil); no depth or figure the rows do not give; never a dig at another trade. On a specification led page: an end post or a strainer leaning as the wires pull on it, so the whole line loses its tension (the stock and chain link rows). On a schedule led page the card is not about a lean: a finish worn through on the weather side first, from the signs row.
cards.mechanism: a post moving in its hole

cards.title: Patched before and gone again
cards.brief: A panel replaced last year that is out again, a post propped with a stake, a gate rehung twice. The one cause this card makes: the failed part left in place under a new one, so the new part fails the same way (the trade facts done badly row for fence repairs: a panel replaced without the failed post behind it). Say when a repair is worth it and when it is not, from the fence repairs row: a repair keeps a run whose other posts are firm; where the posts along the run have all gone soft, the next repair is the next weak post. On a concrete posts and gravel boards page the card is the timber post or board replaced like for like more than once, and what a concrete post or board changes (the stages and materials for that service; no lifespan figure, because the facts verify none). On a specification led page: mesh pulled tight again on a strainer that has itself moved. On a schedule led page: a coat put on over a peeling one, or on damp timber, that lifts within the season (the staining done badly row). Never a dig at another trade.
cards.mechanism: the failed part left in place under a new one

cards.title: Trouble at the bottom of the fence
cards.brief: Where the fence meets the ground: a panel's lower edge gone soft, a gap scraped under the gate, the bottom wire of the mesh lifted, a gravel board cracked (the trade facts signs rows). The one cause this card makes: the lowest part of the fence sitting on or in the soil, where it stays wet, or where an animal works at it. What the job does about it, from the stages and the fact row on gravel boards: a gravel board keeping the panel off the ground, the bottom edge of the mesh secured, the gate detail closed up for that dog. Not a post gone soft at the ground: the category page owns that. On a specification led page: the stock sized opening at the bottom of a run, the loose bottom edge a dog goes under, the bottom wire of chain link that has lost its tension. On a schedule led page: the cut ends and the lowest boards that soak up the wet first, from the signs row.
cards.mechanism: the lowest part of the fence sitting on the soil

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission for [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts rule rows for this service only, put as what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases". For a fence or a gate: the condition that brings a rule in (a boundary beside a road with traffic on it, where the lower height applies and its pavement counts; the higher height everywhere else, taken from the ground with any trellis counted in; a replacement that keeps an existing greater height; a listed home; an estate where the right has been taken away; a conservation area, where taking an old boundary down can need permission). For automatic gates: the new electrical circuit is the part that is notified, and the finished gate is tested for force and fitted with its safety devices before it is handed over. For agricultural, stock and equestrian fencing: the countryside hedge rules on taking a hedge out and on when it is cut. For temporary fencing: consent where the pavement or the road is occupied. The heights only as the rows give them and only where the rows are in the prompt. What the customer does only as the row gives it. Never a standard's number, an Act's or an order's name, or legal advice. Where the rows give no rule, say no permission is usually needed for this work at a home and leave it there.

faq_slots.question: What does your [SERVICE_LOWER] service include?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The What's Included items said as a sentence, in other words: the work itself, named (the line set out, the posts dug and set, the boards or panels fitted, the old fence taken out where that practice is confirmed). What it does not cover only from the services list, with one sibling service page or the category page linked. Never 'on this page' or 'listed above': name the work.

faq_symptom.frame: [SYMPTOM]: why does it happen, and what can be done?
faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom (a leaning run, posts rotting at the ground, panels blowing out, a gate that drags) and its linked local issue, answered as asked. Say first when it is normal (new timber silvering, a panel that rattles in a gale and is back in its slot by morning) and then what is not. Then the usual cause here in the wind, the ground or the timber, in plain words; what the local exposure or soil adds only from the research; and what this service does about it. One figure at most.

problem_card.title: What a wet winter leaves in the ground
problem_card.brief: What shows in spring after the cold wet months, from the trade facts signs row for this service: a post that now rocks, a panel sitting lower in its slot, a gate that has dropped, a bottom board gone soft. Say first what is normal after a winter (timber dark and green on the shaded face, a run that creaks in the wind and settles again) and then what is not. The one cause this card makes: wet winter ground softening round the posts, so what was firm in autumn moves by spring. Not the wind finding a weak post: the category page owns that. Say what gets looked at in spring from confirmed practices only; otherwise what the job puts right, from the stages. On a schedule led page: the coat checked once the timber has dried out in spring and put on in a dry spell under the maker's conditions (the staining stages and timing cell).
problem_card.mechanism: wet winter ground softening round the posts

faq_slot.question: When is the best time of year for [SERVICE_LOWER], and how long does it take?
faq_slot.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing row only: fencing goes in all year where the ground allows it; what the season changes, in the ground, the concrete or the timber (post concrete sets more slowly in the cold; staining waits for dry timber and the maker's weather; a hedge along the line is checked for nests before it is cut back); then the duration, which the row gives for no fencing job, so what decides it instead. No dates, no promises about the weather. This is the one place the timing is written.

cards.title: Who can see in, and who could get out
cards.brief: The customer's situation: next door's upstairs windows look onto where they sit, a toddler or a dog with a way through to the road, a front garden with nothing between the lawn and the pavement, bins stood against the house wall. What decides it: what the boundary has to do for this household (cover where they sit, keep a dog or a child in, mark the front without closing it off, hide the bins) and the height that usually applies there (lower beside a road with traffic on it, its pavement included; higher elsewhere), from the trade facts rule rows as what usually applies, never the order's name, no figure the rows do not give. What the work gives them, from the stages and materials for this service: a solid closeboard or panel run where they sit, picket or railings at the front, a gate that latches, a store with a door that shuts. Never a fault invented for it, never a lifestyle pitch, never security sold on fear.
cards.mechanism: what the boundary has to do for this household

cards.title: An exposed run or a sheltered one
cards.brief: The customer's situation: the garden is on the edge of the estate, up the hill or with an open field behind it, or tucked in among houses that break the wind. What decides it: how much wind the run takes. A solid fence takes the whole of it; boards fixed alternately on the two faces let the wind pass between them (the hit and miss row); prefabricated panels do not suit the most exposed runs (the fact row on exposed locations, no figure); closeboard is built board by board on site, so it is made to the run. What holds it up decides the rest: the posts set for the height and the exposure, the concrete or the gravel board keeping timber off the wet soil (the stages and materials for this service; no depth the rows do not give). What the work gives them: a run chosen for its exposure, not the one in the catalogue. Never storm proof, never a promise about the wind.
cards.mechanism: how much wind the run takes

cards.title: Timber, concrete, composite or metal
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they are weighing two or three ways of doing it (timber posts against concrete, closeboard against panels, timber against composite, timber against metal railings, a manual gate against an automatic one). What decides it: what it stands next to (a cottage front, a modern estate, a drive), the ground (a timber post is trimmed on the day to follow a slope; concrete ones arrive at one size; a concrete post does not rot where it meets the soil, and a slotted one takes a new panel without digging), and the upkeep they want (timber recoated as the maker says; composite only within its maker's system; metal with its coating kept whole, since rust starts where the coating is broken), from the trade facts materials cells and done badly rows for the services on the page. What the work gives them: the material that suits their boundary, never the one that is best in general. A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. No lifespan or guarantee claim: the facts verify none for closeboard against panels or for composite, and a maker's post guarantee covers the post, not the fence.
cards.mechanism: the look, the ground and the upkeep deciding the material

cards.title: Whose fence it is, and which way it faces
cards.brief: The customer's situation: the project customer's worry about a falling out with next door. What decides it: whose boundary it is and where the line runs, from the trade facts fact rows: there is no rule that the fence on the left or the right is yours; the deeds decide; a T mark on a plan can show who looks after a boundary but does not settle it on its own; the title plan shows a general line, not where each post stands; the finished face turned outward is a custom, not a law. What the work gives them: the line agreed before a hole is dug (the set out stage; on the made to measure page, the row's check of the boundary and permissions) and, as the customer's part, a word with next door before anything comes down. Never legal advice, never a guess at which side owns it, never a promise about the neighbour.
cards.mechanism: a boundary shared with next door

problem_card.title: Getting it up in the right weather
problem_card.brief: The customer's situation: they want the garden closed in before the summer, or want to know when it should go up. What decides it: the conditions the job waits for, from the trade facts timing cells for this service (fencing goes in all year where the ground allows; post concrete sets more slowly in the cold; a coating goes on only when the timber is dry and the maker's weather holds; a composite system within its maker's conditions; a hedge along the line checked for nests before it is cut back). What the work gives them: a fence put up when the ground and the timber will take it, so the posts stay put. No dates, nothing about spring being busy or booking ahead, no promise about the weather.
problem_card.mechanism: the ground and the timber the job waits for

faq_slot.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing row only: fencing goes in all year where the ground allows it; what the season changes, in the ground, the concrete or the timber; then the duration, which the row gives for no fencing job, so what decides it instead. No dates, no promises about the weather. This is the one place the timing is written.

cards.title: Runs that catch the wind
cards.brief: Fences on the edge of town, up on the hill, along a coastal front or with open fields behind, where the town profile gives the exposure. The one cause this card makes: the town's open edges and exposed estates, where a run takes the full wind with nothing to break it. Say what it means for the work, never for anyone's fence: how the posts are set for that exposure, why a solid panel is the wrong choice on the most exposed runs and boards fixed alternately or closeboard built on site suit them (the trade facts fact row on exposed locations; no figure, no wind rating). Never a named storm the research does not give, never that the town's fences are blowing down. Not a post gone soft at the ground, not the wind finding a weak post: the town's category and service pages own those.
cards.mechanism: the town's open edges and exposed estates

cards.title: Ground that works posts loose
cards.brief: Posts that rock after a dry summer, holes that fill with water as they are dug, digging that hits stone a spade's depth down, where the town profile gives the ground. The one cause this card makes: the ground under the town's gardens: clay that shrinks as it dries and swells when wet, so a post set in it moves; sandy ground that gives; stony ground that slows every hole; low ground where the water is close under the surface. Say what it means for setting posts, in plain words; no depth or figure (the facts verify no universal post depth); never promise the ground will change. Not a post sitting in wet soil and rotting: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: the ground under the town's gardens

cards.title: Boundaries from when the streets were built
cards.brief: Chain link between the back gardens of a post war estate, a concrete post run from the eighties, a wall and railings on a Victorian street, open plan fronts with no boundary at all, where the town profile dates the housing. The one cause this card makes: fences put up with the houses, built for how the street was lived in then. Tie the era to the work, never to a judgement on the fences: a run of that age comes out with its posts and their concrete before anything new goes in (the trade facts removal stages and price rows); on an open plan estate the right to fence the front may have been taken away, said as sometimes and only where the research confirms it. Where the boundary is shared, a word with next door comes first; whose it is comes from the deeds, never from left or right. What the business does only from confirmed practices.
cards.mechanism: fences put up with the houses

cards.title: Front gardens beside the road
cards.brief: Front gardens that meet a road with traffic on it, or its pavement, where the town profile gives the street pattern. The one cause this card makes: the lower height that usually applies to a boundary beside a road, pavement included, which is why the front fences in these streets are low. What usually applies, from the trade facts rule rows, with usually and never the order's name or a figure the rows do not give: the lower limit at the front, the higher one elsewhere, a conservation area that does not change the heights but can control taking an old boundary down, a listed home that needs a check first. What people put at the front instead: picket, railings, a low wall with a hedge behind it, named only where the services list has the page. Not the overlooked back garden: the category page owns that.
cards.mechanism: the lower height that usually applies beside a road

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] in [TOWN]

cards.title: Carrying it all through the house
cards.brief: Where the back garden is reached only through the house or along a shared side passage, each post, every panel and the bags of concrete is carried by hand and the old fence comes out the same way; the town profile says which streets are terraced. Say why that adds time (never 'the only way': a superlative). No figure.

cards.title: Gardens on a slope
cards.brief: A boundary that falls or rises with the street is stepped bay by bay, each post set to its own level and each panel or board cut to meet the next (the trade facts price rows: changes of level). From the town profile where it gives the slope. No figure.

cards.title: What is in the ground here
cards.brief: Stone a spade's depth down, roots along an old hedge line, buried concrete from the last fence, pipes and cables under the line: what the digging meets in this town, from the profile only, said as what the work meets and never as a judgement on the gardens (the trade facts price rows: difficult ground, buried services, old foundations). No figure.

cards.title: Conservation areas and estate rules
cards.brief: Where the town has conservation areas, listed buildings or estates where the right to fence the front has been taken away, the checks before a boundary at the front can go up add time, and some things need permission first. Usually, never the order's or the area's official name. From the dossier rules only; otherwise a check with the council as something that sometimes applies.

Where the town profile gives the ground (clay still wet in spring, water close under the surface), say what it does to the digging. Nothing about autumn being busy or booking ahead. cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How much fence there is to coat
cards.brief: The length of the run and whether one face or both are being done, the height, the gates and the posts counted in (the trade facts price row: access to both faces, the number of coats the product asks for). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: The state of the timber
cards.brief: Bare new timber, timber gone grey, an old coating peeling that has to come off, green growth to wash off before anything goes on, timber still wet that has to dry first (the trade facts stages: clean and prepare, let the timber dry as the product requires; the price row: surface preparation, how much old coating comes off). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: Getting at both faces and what has to be covered
cards.brief: A fence reached from the garden only or from next door's side as well, a border planted hard against it, a patio, a shed, a wall or a brick pier the brush must keep off, what is sheeted and masked before a coat goes on (the trade facts stages: protect adjoining surfaces; the price row: access to both faces). Say why each adds time. Never a promise about what next door will allow.

cards.title: The stain or treatment you choose
cards.brief: A stain, a paint or a clear preserver, and the number of coats the product asks for; brush against spray only as the trade facts give them. A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. A coat on the surface is not the pressure treatment the posts had at the yard (the trade facts materials cell), so never say it stops a post rotting in the ground, and no wait before coating fresh timber as a rule (the facts verify none). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us About the Fence
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to send first (roughly how long the run is, one face or both, what is on it now, a photo of the worst patch). No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Look at the Timber and Price the Job
steps.brief: The visit and what gets looked at: how dry the timber is, what old coating has to come off, growth to wash off, which faces can be reached and what is planted or built against them. Follows [CV: quote_method]; only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps.title: We Treat It in a Dry Spell That Suits You
steps.brief: The date is agreed in advance, to suit the customer, and it waits for dry timber and the weather the coating maker allows (the trade facts timing cell); no number of dry days, no promise about the weather. A day moved by the rain and rebooked only when the weather_delays_rebooked practice is confirmed. Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan (step 2 and Why choose us own them). Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it).

cards.title: What it has to hold

cards.title: A roof, doors and how it opens
cards.brief: A sloping roof that throws the rain off, a lid that lifts for the bins, doors or an open front, slatted sides so air gets through the logs (the trade facts stages: cladding, roof and doors; the price row: roof and door detailing). Say why each adds work, in plain words.

cards.title: Where it stands and what it fixes to
cards.brief: On paving or a slab that is already there, or on a base that has to be made first; freestanding, or built onto the fence or a wall; how it is reached with the timber (the trade facts stages: measure the location and access, prepare the base; the price row: base preparation, site access). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only. Whether the business lays a base only from the services list or confirmed practices.

cards.title: The timber and the finish
cards.brief: The timber and its treatment, the cladding pattern, a coat of stain or preserver, only from [CV: materials_methods]; what keeps the frame off the wet ground and sheds the rain, because a store stands outside all year (the trade facts done badly row: rain let in by a poor detail, decay where the timber treatment did not suit). No lifespan figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: The gate and what moves it
cards.brief: One leaf against two, sliding against swing, the posts or piers it hangs on, the motor and its safety devices, the power run to it (the trade facts stages: foundations, the gate and its operator, the protective devices; the price row: gate fabrication, the electrical supply and the civil works, the safety device design). Say it plainly and give no figure. Never a brand of motor unless [CV: materials_methods] names it.

cards.brief: An old gate and its posts, piers that are not up to the weight of a powered gate, the foundation for new posts or for a slide track, the trench for the cable across the drive (the trade facts stages: build foundations; the price row: civil works). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.brief: A drive that rises behind the gate so a swing leaf cannot clear it, a drive too short for a leaf to swing in so it slides instead, where the power comes from and how far it has to run, pipes and cables under the line of the trench (the trade facts price row: electrical supply and civil works). Say why each adds time. Who does the electrical work only from the services list or confirmed practices.

cards.title: The gate, the safety kit and the extras
cards.brief: Timber or metal leaves and their finish, an intercom or keypad, a remote for each car, from [CV: materials_methods] only; the safety devices the risk assessment calls for (edges that stop the gate when it meets something, detection so it does not close on a person, the closing force tested at the end) and the paperwork handed over, from the trade facts stages and the done badly row. Say plainly that the safety side is part of the job and never a thing to leave off, with no figure and no standard's number; never say photocells alone make a gate safe (the trade facts fact row).
